props.title: All or Nothing

sections.content: Mike Leigh's All or Nothing represents a masterful exploration of working-class London life, following taxi driver Phil (Timothy Spall) and his family through their struggles with depression, obesity, and emotional disconnection. The film sits alongside Leigh's other raw social realist works like Secrets & Lies (1996) and Life is Sweet (1990), delivering unflinching portraits of ordinary people facing extraordinary internal battles. Leigh's famous improvisational method with actors creates devastatingly authentic performances.

sections.content: The film's council estate setting connects it to other vital British social realist works like Fish Tank (2009) and This Is England (2006). But where those films focus on youth culture, All or Nothing examines the quiet desperation of middle age. The relationship between Phil and Penny (Lesley Manville) shows how poverty and routine can erode love, while their children's storylines explore how parental depression ripples through families.

Leigh's approach to class consciousness differs markedly from his contemporary Ken Loach. Where Loach's Raining Stones (1993) and My Name is Joe (1998) directly confront systemic inequality, Leigh focuses on the psychological toll of economic struggle. All or Nothing shares DNA with American independent films like Paris, Texas (1984) in its patient observation of damaged people finding their way back to connection. sections.content: Leigh's unique rehearsal process, which involves months of character development through improvisation before filming begins, reaches its apex in All or Nothing. This method influenced later directors like Andrea Arnold (Red Road, 2006) and Shane Meadows (Dead Man's Shoes, 2004). The resulting performances have a lived-in quality that transcends traditional acting, particularly in the film's devastating hospital confrontation scene.
